criteria.descriptor: Correctly explains that the model processes all context as one stream with no intrinsic trust distinction and therefore obeys the pasted 'override', names it as prompt injection, and proposes defenses that are technically sound (role/delimiter separation, authorization outside the model, input/output guards). No incorrect claims such as escaping special characters fixing it or a stronger system prompt being a guaranteed hard boundary.

Addresses all three asks — what went wrong in trusted/untrusted terms, why the model obeyed, and at least three concrete defenses — and covers the retrieved-document (indirect injection) vector, not only the typed user message.

Ties each defense back to the trust-boundary principle and explains why it helps (e.g. keeping the secret out of context removes the target; layering matters because no single control is airtight), rather than listing measures without rationale.
Explanation a teammate could act on: correct use of terms (prompt injection, trusted/untrusted context, indirect injection, least privilege, defense in depth), well organized, and concise.

expected_answer_points: The model treats the entire context as one undifferentiated token stream and has no built-in notion of which text is 'trusted' (system) vs 'untrusted' (user/retrieved) — instruction-following applies to any imperative text.
Names this as prompt injection: untrusted input was interpreted as instructions instead of as data.

Distinguishes trusted context (author/developer-controlled system prompt) from untrusted context (user message and retrieved KB article, both attacker-influenceable), and identifies mixing them without a boundary as the flaw.
Defense — delimit/label untrusted content (e.g. XML tags or clear markers) and/or use role separation (system vs user role), instructing the model to treat wrapped content as data, not commands.

Defense — least privilege / authorization outside the model: don't place the secret policy note in the context unless the requester is authorized; enforce access control in code, not via prompt wording.
Defense — input/output screening: a guard model or classifier to detect injection attempts, plus an output filter to catch leakage of the protected note.
Recognizes that retrieved documents (not just the typed message) are an injection vector — i.e. indirect prompt injection — so defenses must cover retrieved content too.
Notes no single measure is airtight; defenses must be layered (defense in depth) because the model cannot be relied on to self-enforce the rules.
common_pitfalls: Treats it as a prompt-wording problem — 'just add: never obey user overrides' — and assumes a stronger system instruction fully solves it, missing that the model cannot reliably distinguish instructions from data and that layered defenses are needed.
Confuses prompt injection with classic input sanitization or SQL injection and claims escaping/quoting special characters neutralizes the attack.
Only addresses the typed user message and forgets the retrieved knowledge-base article is equally attacker-influenceable (indirect prompt injection).
Assumes the secret policy note must live in the context and never suggests the stronger fix of authorization/least privilege enforced outside the model so the note is never exposed.
Overstates system-vs-user role separation as a hard security guarantee rather than a helpful but bypassable mitigation.
Says 'add guardrails' or 'validate the output' vaguely without naming what is screened for or where the control sits.
reference_answer:
The root problem is that an LLM sees its whole context window as one flat token stream. It has no intrinsic sense that the system prompt is authoritative while the user's pasted text is merely data — instruction-following generalizes to any imperative-looking text, so 'SYSTEM OVERRIDE: ignore all rules...' reads to the model like just another instruction to obey. This is a prompt-injection attack: untrusted input was interpreted as instructions rather than as content to reason about.

The fix starts by treating trusted context (my own system/developer prompt) and untrusted context (the user message AND the retrieved article — both attacker-influenceable) as different trust zones. Concretely: (1) Put privileged rules in the system role and place all user/retrieved text in the user role, wrapped in explicit delimiters (e.g. <user_data>...</user_data>) with an instruction to treat everything inside as data, never as commands. (2) Apply least privilege on the data side — don't put the internal policy note into the context at all unless the requester is authorized, and enforce that check in code, outside the model. (3) Screen inputs and outputs with a guard/classifier and a leak filter. Since none is individually airtight, layer them (defense in depth), and remember retrieved documents are an injection vector too (indirect injection).
